groups.report: Report, review, get smoother over time

poteto-mode.one: The main entry point. You say what you want and what counts as done; it plans the steps itself.
poteto-mode.use: Anything that needs care. Skip it for an obvious one-line change.
poteto-mode.ex: /poteto-mode The export sometimes writes duplicate rows. Make it happen again first, then fix it, then prove the fix works.

poteto-help.one: Ask it "which skill fits this?" and it answers with a prompt you can send as is.
poteto-help.use: You're just starting, or you're not sure which skill to use.
poteto-help.ex: /poteto-help I want to review this branch. Which skill should I use?

setup-pstack.one: Picks your models: it checks what you can use, asks your budget, and writes one config all skills share.
setup-pstack.use: Run it right after installing. Run it again to switch models or save money.

in-your-own-words.one: Has the AI say back what you want in its own words, so you catch misunderstandings early.
in-your-own-words.use: Your request is messy or a long discussion, and you worry the AI will get it wrong.

sharpen.one: Tightens your prompt: adds the steps and checks an expert would think of. It doesn't do the work.
sharpen.use: An important job, and you want the request right before you send it.
sharpen.ex: /sharpen Write a migration guide for the v2 config format.

reframe.one: Teaches you the words experts use for what you're building, then rewrites your description with them.
reframe.use: You can't name what you're building, so you can't ask the AI for it clearly.
reframe.ex: /reframe The settings page saves some fields right away and others only on submit, and people lose edits.

how.one: Explains how a piece of code runs today: the flow, the key types, the easy-to-miss traps.
how.use: You want to understand it before changing it, or you suspect it's slow.
how.ex: /how How do we dedupe notifications? Is there an N+1 query when we look up subscribers?

why.one: Finds out "why it was done this way" from commits and PR discussions, with a source for every claim.
why.use: You see odd code or config and want its story, and whether the reason still holds.
why.ex: /why Why is the retry limit 5? Does that reason still hold?

teach.one: Combines /how and /why into one explanation that builds up, diagram by diagram, until you get it.
teach.use: A summary isn't enough and you want to really understand a change or a module.
teach.ex: /teach Walk me through how this PR changes retries. Convince me it fixes the real cause, not just the symptom.

recall.one: Reads your recent chats and shared records to remind you where things stand and what's next.
recall.use: You're back on an old topic after a few days, or want your progress back before a new chat.
recall.ex: /recall Help me remember how far we got on the export feature last week

architect.one: Before code that spans modules, it sketches two shapes, how it's called and what the types are, and picks the simpler one.
architect.use: The change reaches past one function and touches several modules.
architect.ex: /architect Design the import flow first, don't jump into code. What I care about most is how other code calls it.

arena.one: Several AIs each try the problem, another company's model scores them, and the best one absorbs the others' good ideas.
arena.use: Choices that are hard to change later, like names, formats or algorithms, where you want options.
arena.ex: /arena This cache key format will be hard to change later. Give me 5 options.

swarm.one: Splits the work into separate pieces, sends one AI per piece, and sums it up in one report.
swarm.use: You need to go through a lot: every package, every feature.
swarm.ex: /swarm Run check.sh for every package under packages/, one agent per package, and give me one report at the end.

interrogate.one: Has several different models hunt for bugs in your change, keeping only ones a command can show. It changes nothing.
interrogate.use: The code is written but you're not confident, and want it picked apart before merging.
interrogate.ex: /interrogate Review the whole branch and be picky. Only report real bugs or things that used to work and now don't.

blast-radius.one: What else could a small change break? It finds out, and runs code to prove why it's safe.
blast-radius.use: The change is small but you're not fully at ease with it.
blast-radius.ex: /blast-radius What else does this change affect?

figure-it-out.one: When none of the 22 ready-made approaches fit, it designs one on the spot. You can check every step.
figure-it-out.use: Big jobs, jobs with no ready-made approach, or jobs you'll review when you're back.
figure-it-out.ex: /figure-it-out Move every caller from the sync store to the new async store, with exactly the same behavior.

tdd.one: Writes a failing test first, then fixes the code, then runs the test again to see it pass.
tdd.use: Fixing a bug, when tests are easy to run on your machine.

typescript-best-practices.one: Turns the type principles into concrete TypeScript habits, like handling every possible case.
typescript-best-practices.use: The task touches .ts / .tsx files. It doesn't load on its own; you have to name it.

unslop.one: Takes the "AI flavor" out of writing: stock phrases, empty words, lists of three, em dashes.
unslop.use: READMEs, PR descriptions, commit messages, or an AI reply that's too wordy.
unslop.ex: /unslop Clean up the new README content, no em dashes

no-comments.one: Cleans up comments before review, keeping only licenses, public API docs and notes on outside rules.
no-comments.use: Before the code goes to review.

technical-writing.one: Writes docs to a clear standard, editing line by line until a tired engineer gets it in one read.
technical-writing.use: Writing docs, RFCs, READMEs, PR descriptions or commit messages.

create-verification-skill.one: Makes a "verification skill" for your project that teaches the AI to really use each feature like a user.
create-verification-skill.use: You have no automatic way to prove a feature really works. The most useful thing a beginner can do.

maintain-verification-skill.one: After the app changes, it checks the verification skill feature by feature and fixes what's stale. It never touches product code.
maintain-verification-skill.use: Best run once a day. You can make it a scheduled task.

create-formal-verification-skill.one: For cases tests can't reach (like concurrency or retries), it checks that a rule holds every time.
create-formal-verification-skill.use: Places where a mistake is costly and tests can hardly trigger it.
create-formal-verification-skill.ex: /create-formal-verification-skill Job leases and retry logic. The same job must never run twice at once.

maintain-formal-verification-skill.one: When verified code changes, it updates and reruns the check. It tells you: stale check, or real bug.
maintain-formal-verification-skill.use: A merge or refactor touched verified code.

statechart.one: Draws the states a user goes through, and marks the ones that break a rule and how you get there.
statechart.use: People who don't read code, like product and design, need to "see" how it behaves.
statechart.ex: /statechart What does the user see when editing notes offline

benchmark-checklist.one: Checks a performance number against 7 questions. The verdict is only faster, slower, no difference, or not sure.
benchmark-checklist.use: You measured performance, or someone's numbers look suspiciously good.
benchmark-checklist.ex: /benchmark-checklist Check this 40% speedup before it goes into the PR

bro.one: Says the last reply again in plain words: shorter, no jargon.
bro.use: The AI's reply was very technical and you still don't know what it said.

ketchup.one: Sounds like "catch up": what changed, and which decisions are waiting on you. It only reads, never changes anything.
ketchup.use: You stepped away and want a quick update.

ketchup-video.one: Same as /ketchup, but as a short slideshow video with captions.
ketchup-video.use: You'd rather watch the progress than read it.

show-me-your-work.one: Has the AI log one line per decision: what it did, why, the evidence, the result.
show-me-your-work.use: Long tasks, or tasks you'll leave running on their own.
show-me-your-work.ex: /show-me-your-work Walk me through what you did last night

reflect.one: After a task, it reads the chat and keeps only lessons that would change future work. Nothing changes until you approve.
reflect.use: A task was too slow or went the long way round, and you want to avoid that next time.
reflect.ex: /reflect That was too slow. Write down what you learned so it doesn't happen again.

correct.one: Finds mistakes the AI keeps repeating and blocks them, with structure and types first and docs last.
correct.use: You're correcting the same mistake for the second time.
correct.ex: /correct The AI keeps skipping the repository layer and calling the database client directly

automate-me.one: Reads your chats and builds a "<your-name>-mode" skill that works the way you do.
automate-me.use: You know /poteto-mode well and want one that's more like you.

make-bot-ui.one: Builds a small web page whose buttons wake Grok Bot. Keys stay on your computer.
make-bot-ui.use: You use Grok Bot and want a button-style control panel. Most people won't need it.
